title: Reaction to being named an NEA Jazz Master
summary: Burton says the honor was not a total surprise given friends already honored, and that recognition from peers means more than Grammys or polls.

story.community_name: Being honored: NEA Jazz Masters and other awards

blocks.x: Ok. I saw you two or three weeks ago. You had just been honored NEA Jazz Master. What was that feeling... Tell me your reaction when you first learned you became an NEA Jazz Master.

Well, it was not a total surprise, because I’ve watched quite a few of my friends and co-performers, collaborators—Carla Bley, Chick Corea, Keith Jarrett and so on—be given this honor in recent years. So I’ve said to myself, “Well, there’s probably a chance that I might get called one of these days.” So it didn’t totally come out of the blue, but nonetheless felt great to hear that I had been chosen for my career, for my life, to be honored in this way. Other people have asked me about what it means. One thing I can say is how it compares a little bit to winning the Grammy awards, which I’ve been lucky to do sometimes. You get a lot of recognition over the course of your career, awards from poll-winning and all that sort of thing. But when it’s your peers, or experts in the field who declare you a winner, then it means a lot more, and you feel, “Ok, now, this is a real verified accomplishment.” And it felt that way with the Jazz Masters.
